findings.claim: Synchronous `existsSync`/`mkdirSync` are used inside an otherwise async method, blocking the event loop, and the `existsSync` guard is redundant with `recursive: true`.
findings.rationale: `mkdirSync(path, { recursive: true })` is already a no-op when the directory exists, so the `existsSync` guard adds nothing except a TOCTOU race window. Since this is an `async` method that already awaits `writeFile`, `await mkdir(this.rootCache, { recursive: true })` would avoid blocking the main thread. Confident about the redundancy; the blocking concern is a real but modest perf issue.

findings.claim: Only `this.rootCache` is created, but `this.metadataFilePath` may live in a nested subdirectory, in which case `writeFile` will still fail with ENOENT.
findings.rationale: The directory creation assumes `metadataFilePath` is a direct child of `rootCache`. If the metadata path is nested deeper (or derived differently), the mkdir won't create the needed parent and the write silently fails through the catch. Safer to `mkdir(dirname(this.metadataFilePath), { recursive: true })`. I cannot see the field definitions in this hunk, so this is a suspicion rather than a confirmed bug.

findings.claim: Non-atomic write of the metadata file can leave a truncated/corrupt file that a concurrent or subsequent reader interprets as "no metadata".
findings.rationale: `writeFile` truncates then writes; if the process is killed mid-write, or two Vitest instances share the same cache root, a reader gets partial JSON. The reader swallows the parse error (`catch {}`), so the failure mode is a silent full cache invalidation. Writing to a temp file and `rename`-ing would make it atomic. Moderate confidence this matters in practice when multiple projects share one cache dir.

findings.claim: Completely swallowing write failures means the cache-integrity check can never converge: every subsequent run will see a missing/stale lockfile hash and nuke the cache.
findings.rationale: The comment frames this as best-effort, which is reasonable for not aborting the run, but a persistent failure (e.g. read-only FS, permission error) degrades silently into "cache is always cold" with only a debug-level message. Consider a one-time warn, or distinguishing EACCES/EROFS from transient errors. Low-to-moderate confidence this rises above intentional design.

findings.claim: `debugFs?.(`...${error}`)` is the only error surface and stringifying the error loses the stack trace.
findings.rationale: `${error}` yields only `Error: message` with no stack, making diagnosis hard for the one place this code reports problems; if `debugFs` is undefined the failure is entirely invisible. Passing the error object (or `error.stack`) would retain context. Minor but directly affects debuggability of a silently-failing path.

findings.claim: New code depends on `existsSync`, `mkdirSync`, and `writeFile` being imported; if any are not already in scope the change will not compile.
findings.rationale: The hunk adds three fs API usages but shows no import changes. The file previously did async reads, so `writeFile` from `node:fs/promises` and the sync helpers from `node:fs` may or may not already be imported. Flagging for verification only — cannot confirm from the shown context.
